chapters.s: The circle of laughter that formed the threshold of the dream court had followed Batuknath since evening. The laughter of Channa Grove rang all night in Batuknath Hariharan's ears. That night, when the stump of Channa Grove laughed again, the laughter did not stop at Batuknath's house. It climbed an invisible wire and entered Chandrapal Batra's screen.

“The turn of the man of percentages”—this unwritten notice in the stump's laughter had found its destination by morning. The night of Batuknath Hariharan's dream court had passed, but its dust had not settled on his head alone. The stump of Channa Grove fell silent again that night. But its silence carried a clear message: the first confession is not the end of punishment, only the latch of a door. Beyond that door sat Raghav Signal without a network.

Beyond that door—in a glass room in the city—sat Raghav, who possessed everything except reach. For the first time in his life, Raghav “Signal” Somani felt that the greatest deprivation in the world was not money, power, access or cunning, but network. At that very moment in Channa Grove, Ananya closed the register and said, “Today a distant name moved.” The children asked, “What now?” Ananya looked at the green point on the stump. During the night it had lengthened a little.…

The shadow that had turned its face toward Mithila was now beginning to take bodily form. Raghav Signal's night without a network travelled all the way to Lau Kin-Hung's city. The interpreter did not understand the sentence. But far behind them, in the airport glass, the crocodile's eye truly blinked.

The first step through the door opened by that blinking crocodile's eye lay inside the airport itself. Lau Kin-Hung's plane landed between night and dawn. Thus the crocodile at the airport did not chew Lau's body; it stripped off the first skin of his sense of security. He had arrived in India as a businessman, but as he moved toward the waiting hall his shadow belonged to a man who could no longer flee his own…

chapters.t: The Silent Dialogue of Satyavrat and Lau
chapters.s: The road opened by the message from the waiting hall led directly to Channa Grove. After seeing the crocodile's eye in the airport glass, Lau Kin-Hung did not sleep all night. Satyavrat Mehta did not smile. Nor did Lau Kin-Hung. From inside the stump came a faint rattling—not laughter, not weeping, only notice that the next trial had begun.

The notice of the next trial that had sounded in the stump's rattling reached the village at dawn as a thick postal packet. The morning after Lau Kin-Hung's silent dialogue, the packet arrived in Garh Narikel. And from the wet smell of the deed was born the next question—if a father sold justice and earned prestige, would his child inherit that prestige or become a witness to his crime? Channa Grove's laughter had stopped.…

Tarini confronts Batuknath Hariharan with the question of whether his profession served justice or merely preserved authority. Her challenge forces the Public Memory Trust toward public scrutiny, while Chandrapal, alone elsewhere, struggles even to write his own full name—signalling that inherited power is beginning to fracture from within.

The waiting court was not convened in a hall but within the boundary of a white sheet of paper. The question Hariharan's daughter had asked her father that night—"Did you save justice or the profession?"—echoed far beyond Garh Narikel. He could not tell whether this was dream or punishment. But in Garh Narikel, at that very moment, Ananya closed the register and said, "Next time the elephant-and-crocodile within will play." A shiver ran through all the children's bodies at once.…
chapters.tu: hopeful rhythm of the elephant-and-crocodile tale

chapters.s: "Next time the elephant-and-crocodile within will play"—Ananya's sentence found its field the very next evening. The question from Hariharan's child, Batra's incomplete name, Raghav without a network, the crocodile Lau Kin-Hung had seen in glass—these were no longer separate events. That morning Ananya opened a new page of the register and wrote the heading: "Coconut-Leaf School." The green point on the stump spread a little. From afar Old Budhba's Ghost released the breath of kabaddi—"Kabaddi..." and the children answered…

The game that had descended into study during the night began, by morning, to take the form of earth and leaves. After the night's elephant-and-crocodile within had subsided, morning in Garh Narikel was not ordinary. The chapter ended in that expectation. The Coconut-Leaf School had been made, but its first lesson was still waiting to open. The empty bowl remained in the centre.…

That heading in the register—“First Lesson: Present”—became its own first bell in the morning light. On the first day after the Coconut-Leaf School opened, no one studied the alphabet. The green point on the stump glowed faintly in the darkness. The school's first lesson did not end; it began turning into a night assembly. The children closed the register but left the blank page open.…

The page left open did not spend the night merely waiting—it summoned its own assembly as soon as evening fell. The first lesson of the Coconut-Leaf School, “Present,” had been taught by day; but the word's true body opened at night. Before sunrise the women left, but around the stump remained the smell of red thread, the dampness of the shirt, the weight of the blank page and the dust of cracked heels.…

By morning the story that had turned took the road—from the village to the half-built bridge. After the republic of names completed its first lesson, the children felt that saying “Present” did not finish the story. As she walked home Ananya said, “Tomorrow the school will have no screens.” Devika asked, “Why?” Ananya replied, “Today we read feet. Tomorrow we must open the eyes and ears again.…
